tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 2. Our Solar System. On 14 July 2015, a spacecraft about the size of a grand piano flew roughly 12,500 kilometers above the surface of Pluto. Its radio signals, traveling at the speed of light, needed about four and a half hours to reach Earth. The pictures showed a world nobody had expected: mountains of water ice several kilometers high, a huge pale region shaped like a heart, and a wide plain of frozen nitrogen with no impact craters at all, which means its surface is young. There was a twist in the story. When that spacecraft, New Horizons, left Earth in January 2006, Pluto was the ninth planet. Seven months later, the world’s astronomers voted to call it something else. To see why, you first need to meet the whole family of the Sun. Chapter 1 kept your feet on the ground: you watched the sky turn, the Moon change shape and the seasons come and go. This chapter goes out into space one stop at a time. Section 2.1 visits the four rocky planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Section 2.2 crosses a wide gap to the four giant planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, and shows which planets you can find with your own eyes. Section 2.3 meets the smaller members of the family: moons, asteroids, comets and the dwarf planets, including Pluto and the reason it was reclassified in 2006. Along the way you will extend the pocket scale model, in which the Sun is a ball about 20 cm (8 inches) across and Earth is a peppercorn 24 m (26 yards) away, to every planet, and you will add a planet to your sky diary.

tracks.label: 2.1 Rocky planets
tracks.text: Section 2 point 1. Rocky planets. The Sun holds about 99.8 percent of all the mass in the solar system; the planets and everything else are the small change. The planets travel around the Sun on nearly circular paths called orbits, all lying close to one flat plane, which is why the Sun, the Moon and the planets all stay close to the ecliptic, the line across our sky that you met in Chapter 1. Distances out here are so large that kilometers become clumsy, so astronomers use the astronomical unit (AU), the average distance from Earth to the Sun: about 149.6 million kilometers. Light, the fastest thing there is, takes about 8.3 minutes to cross one AU. The eight planets fall into two clear families. The four closest to the Sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small worlds of rock and metal with solid surfaces you could stand on. Astronomers call them the terrestrial planets, from terra, Latin for Earth. Nobody has drilled into another planet, yet we know what the rocky planets are made of. One strong clue is density, the amount of mass packed into each cubic centimeter. Astronomers weigh a planet by timing how strongly it pulls on its moons or on a passing spacecraft, and they measure its size directly; mass divided by volume gives density. Water has a density of 1 gram per cubic centimeter, ordinary rock about 3, and iron nearly 8. The four rocky planets come out between about 3.9 (Mars) and 5.5 (Earth), too dense to be rock all the way through, so each must have a rocky outer layer around a heavy iron core. The same test gives a very different answer for the giant planets in section 2.2. Mercury is the smallest planet, 4,879 km across, a little more than a third of Earth’s width, and the closest to the Sun at an average of 0.39 AU. It races around the Sun in just 88 days. Mercury has almost no air to hold heat in, so its surface swings from above 400 degrees Celsius in the daytime to below minus 150 degrees Celsius at night. Its surface is covered in craters, bowl-shaped scars left by impacts, much like the Moon’s. NASA’s MESSENGER spacecraft, which orbited Mercury from 2011 to 2015, found strong evidence for something unexpected so close to the Sun: water ice inside craters near the poles, where the crater floors never see sunlight. From Earth, Mercury never strays far from the Sun in our sky, so you can catch it only low in the twilight, just after sunset or just before sunrise. Venus is almost Earth’s twin in size, 12,104 km across, but it is the least welcoming of the rocky planets. Its air is about 96 percent carbon dioxide and so thick that the pressure at the ground is about 90 times the pressure on Earth, like being nearly a kilometer deep in the ocean. The carbon dioxide traps heat, an extreme case of the greenhouse effect, and holds the surface at about 465 degrees Celsius day and night, hot enough to melt lead. That makes Venus hotter than Mercury, even though it is nearly twice as far from the Sun. Clouds of sulfuric acid droplets hide the ground, so NASA’s Magellan spacecraft mapped it by radar, and the Soviet Venera landers that reached the surface survived only minutes to about two hours. Venus also spins backward, so slowly that one turn takes 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year. Earth is the largest of the rocky planets, 12,756 km across, the only world known to have oceans of liquid water on its surface and the only place where life is known to exist. Now place the rocky planets in the pocket scale model you began in Chapter 1. With the Sun as a ball about 20 cm (8 inches) across, Earth is a peppercorn 2 mm wide, 24 m (26 yards) away, and the Moon is a speck smaller than a pinhead about 6 cm from the peppercorn. Mercury is a pinhead 9 m (10 yards) from the Sun, Venus another peppercorn at 17 m (19 yards), and Mars a slightly larger pinhead at 37 m (40 yards). Four tiny specks inside a circle you could walk across in a minute: that is the whole inner solar system. Mars is about half Earth’s width, 6,792 km across, and orbits at 1.52 AU, taking 687 days to go around the Sun. Its day is only a little longer than ours, about 24 hours 40 minutes. The red color you can see with your bare eyes comes from iron oxide, which is rust, in its dust. The air is thin carbon dioxide, with a surface pressure less than 1 percent of Earth’s, yet Mars has the largest volcano known, Olympus Mons, more than twice as tall as Mount Everest, and a canyon system, Valles Marineris, about 4,000 km long. Dry river channels and layered sediments show that water once flowed there. NASA’s Curiosity rover, which landed in Gale crater in 2012, found mudstone laid down in an ancient lake whose water could have supported microbes, if any existed. Mars has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos. A common misconception: Mercury is the hottest planet because it is the closest to the Sun. In fact, Venus is hotter, at about 465 degrees Celsius everywhere on its surface, day and night. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat through the greenhouse effect. Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its daytime side gets above 400 degrees Celsius but its night side drops below minus 150 degrees Celsius.

tracks.label: 2.2 Giant planets
tracks.text: Section 2 point 2. Giant planets. Beyond Mars the spacing changes completely. In the pocket model, Mars sits 37 m (40 yards) from the Sun, but Jupiter, the next planet, sits 123 m (135 yards) out, nearly 90 more meters of almost empty space with only scattered dust grains, the asteroids of section 2.3, in between. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are the giant planets; the smallest of them, Neptune, is still almost four times as wide as Earth. They have no solid surface to land on. Their outer layers are gas that becomes denser and hotter with depth until it behaves like a liquid. Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium, so they are called gas giants. Uranus and Neptune contain a much larger share of water, methane and ammonia, which planetary scientists call ices even when they are hot fluids deep inside, so they are called ice giants. Density tells the same kind of story it told for the rocky planets. Jupiter’s density is about 1.3 grams per cubic centimeter, only a quarter of Earth’s, and Saturn’s is about 0.7, less than water. No rocky world could be that light; these planets must be made mostly of the lightest elements. They are also enormous. Jupiter is 142,984 km across, about 11 times Earth’s width, and has 318 times Earth’s mass, two and a half times as much as all the other planets put together. It spins once in under 10 hours, which flattens it slightly and draws its clouds into the colored bands you can see in a small telescope. Among them is the Great Red Spot, a storm wider than Earth that astronomers have watched for more than 150 years. Jupiter takes 11.9 years to orbit the Sun. Saturn, 120,536 km across, is the second-largest planet; it orbits at about 9.6 AU and takes 29.4 years to circle the Sun. Its rings are made of countless separate pieces of mostly water ice, from dust-sized grains to chunks as big as a house, each orbiting Saturn like a tiny moon. The main rings span about 270,000 km, about 70 percent of the distance from Earth to the Moon, yet they are typically only about 10 meters thick. NASA’s Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, and the European Huygens probe it carried landed on Saturn’s largest moon, Titan, in January 2005. In the pocket model, Saturn is a hazelnut or an acorn, almost 2 cm (about 0.7 inch) across, 226 m (247 yards) from the Sun, with rings about 4 cm wide. Uranus was the first planet discovered with a telescope. William Herschel, a musician and amateur astronomer in Bath, England, spotted it in 1781; every planet out to Saturn had been known since ancient times. Uranus is 51,118 km across, four times Earth’s width, and orbits at about 19.2 AU, taking 84 years to go around the Sun. Methane gas in its upper atmosphere absorbs red light, which leaves its pale blue-green color. Its strangest feature is its tilt. Chapter 1 showed that Earth’s tilt of 23.4 degrees gives us seasons. Uranus is tipped over by about 98 degrees, so it rolls around the Sun on its side. Near each pole there are about 42 years of continuous daylight, then about 42 years of night. Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus: Voyager 2, which flew past in January 1986. Neptune was found with mathematics before anyone saw it. By the 1840s astronomers knew that Uranus was drifting off its predicted path, as if an unseen planet were pulling on it. The French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier calculated where that planet should be, and on 23 September 1846 Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory found Neptune within about one degree of the predicted spot. In England, John Couch Adams had made a similar calculation. Neptune is 49,528 km across and orbits at about 30 AU, so sunlight takes about four hours to reach it. A year there lasts about 164 Earth years. Neptune has the fastest winds measured on any planet, up to about 2,000 km per hour, clocked by Voyager 2 when it flew past in 1989. In the pocket model, Uranus and Neptune are peanuts or coffee beans about 8 mm (0.3 inch) across, 454 m (496 yards) and 711 m (777 yards) from the Sun. Five planets are easy to see with no equipment at all: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. People have watched them for thousands of years, and the word planet comes from the Greek word for wanderer, because these points of light drift against the background stars from week to week. As Chapter 1 noted, they stay close to the ecliptic and usually shine with a steadier light than stars. Venus is the brightest, Jupiter usually comes next, Mars glows orange-red and is brightest about every 26 months, when Earth overtakes it, and Saturn looks like a steady yellowish star. Uranus is at the very limit of naked-eye vision, visible only from a dark site if you know exactly where to look, and Neptune always needs binoculars or a telescope. Steady binoculars also show Jupiter’s four largest moons as tiny points lined up beside it, the same moons Galileo saw in 1610. A common misconception: Saturn is the only planet with rings. In fact, All four giant planets have rings. Uranus’s were found in 1977 when they briefly dimmed a star passing behind them, Jupiter’s faint rings were found by Voyager 1 in 1979, and Neptune’s were confirmed by Voyager 2 in 1989. Saturn’s are simply the brightest, because they are wide and made mostly of reflective water ice.

tracks.label: 2.3 Moons, asteroids, comets and dwarf planets
tracks.text: Section 2 point 3. Moons, asteroids, comets and dwarf planets. A moon is a natural body that orbits a planet, or another smaller body, rather than orbiting the Sun directly. Mercury and Venus have none, Earth has one and Mars has two, but the giant planets have dozens or hundreds. As of 2025, NASA listed more than 90 known moons for Jupiter, 274 for Saturn, 29 for Uranus and 16 for Neptune, and the totals for Jupiter and Saturn have kept rising as telescopes find ever smaller objects. Most of these moons are lumps of rock and ice only a few kilometers across. A few are worlds in their own right. Jupiter’s Ganymede (5,268 km) and Saturn’s Titan (5,150 km) are both wider than the planet Mercury, although Mercury has about twice Ganymede’s mass. Our own Moon, 3,475 km across, is the fifth-largest moon in the solar system. Galileo discovered Jupiter’s four largest moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, in January 1610; they were the first objects ever seen orbiting another planet. Io is the most volcanically active world known, heated from inside as Jupiter’s gravity squeezes and flexes it. Europa and Saturn’s small moon Enceladus almost certainly hide oceans of salty liquid water under their icy crusts, and Cassini flew through jets of water ice spraying from Enceladus’s south pole. Titan has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane; in 2005 the Huygens probe landed there, still the most distant landing ever made. Neptune’s largest moon, Triton, orbits in the opposite direction to Neptune’s spin, a sign that Neptune probably captured it from the Kuiper Belt. NASA’s Europa Clipper, launched in October 2024, is on its way to study whether Europa’s ocean could support life. Asteroids are rocky or metallic bodies left over from the time the planets formed, about 4.6 billion years ago, that never grew into planets. More than a million are known. Most orbit in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, roughly 2.2 to 3.2 AU from the Sun. The largest, Ceres, 940 km across, was also the first found, by Giuseppe Piazzi on 1 January 1801. Movies show a crowded field of tumbling boulders, but the asteroids are so far apart that many spacecraft, starting with Pioneer 10 in 1972, have crossed the belt safely, and together they add up to only a few percent of our Moon’s mass. In the pocket model the whole belt is a few specks of dust scattered around a ring 50 to 75 m from the Sun. When a small piece of rock from space burns up in our air, its streak of light is a meteor; a piece that survives to reach the ground is a meteorite. Comets are mixtures of ice, dust and rock, typically a few kilometers across, that spend most of their time far from the Sun. Near the Sun, sunlight turns some of the ice to gas, which streams off with dust to form a glowing cloud around the solid core, the nucleus, and long tails that point away from the Sun. The European Space Agency’s Rosetta spacecraft orbited comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko from 2014 to 2016 and set a small lander, Philae, down on it. Halley’s Comet returns about every 76 years; it last passed in 1986 and will be back in 2061. Comets also leave trails of dust along their orbits, and when Earth crosses a trail each year the grains burn up as a meteor shower: the Perseids every August come from comet Swift–Tuttle. Comets with very long orbits come from the Oort Cloud, a vast shell of icy bodies thousands of AU away that has never been seen directly. Pluto was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh, a 24-year-old assistant at Lowell Observatory in Arizona, and for 76 years it was counted as the ninth planet. It is far smaller than first thought, 2,377 km across, less than our Moon, and its orbit is so stretched that from 1979 to 1999 it was closer to the Sun than Neptune. In 1992 David Jewitt and Jane Luu found a small object beyond Neptune, first designated 1992 QB1 and now named Albion, the first known member, after Pluto and its moon Charon, of a whole region of icy bodies, the Kuiper Belt, which stretches from about 30 to 50 AU. Thousands are now known, and Pluto is one of the largest. In 2005 a team led by Mike Brown announced Eris, which is almost as wide as Pluto, and in 2007 the orbit of its moon showed that Eris has about 27 percent more mass than Pluto. Astronomers had to decide whether there were ten planets, many more, or fewer. On 24 August 2006, in Prague, the International Astronomical Union (IAU), the world body of professional astronomers, adopted a definition. A planet is a body that (a) orbits the Sun, (b) has enough mass that its own gravity has pulled it into a nearly round shape, and (c) has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit, meaning it is by far the dominant body in its orbital zone. A dwarf planet meets the first two conditions but not the third, and is not a moon. Pluto orbits the Sun and is round, but it shares its zone with many Kuiper Belt objects and crosses Neptune’s orbit, so it fails the third test, while each of the eight planets far outweighs everything else in its zone. The IAU recognizes five dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. Some planetary scientists, including New Horizons leader Alan Stern, still argue that any round body orbiting the Sun should count as a planet, so the debate goes on. A common misconception: Pluto got kicked out because it is too small to be a planet. In fact, Size is not one of the IAU’s tests. Pluto is big enough to be round, which is the size-related condition it does meet. It was reclassified because it has not cleared its orbital zone: it shares it with many other Kuiper Belt objects. Mercury is smaller than Ganymede, yet it is a planet because it dominates its orbit.
